extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and distinctions for when a generalization or hypothesis counts as induction versus mere description/colligation, including what makes evidence sufficient, the role of hypotheses, and the aims (explanation/prediction) of induction. Useful for assessing the legitimacy of inductive reasoning in scientific and philosophical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction vs 'all known' generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: A conclusion that asserts more than 'all known' instances — i.e., that observations reveal a law applicable to yet-undiscovered cases — is required for genuine induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If by saying 'all animals have a nervous system' one means merely 'all known animals,' that is not induction. True induction is when the general proposition contains more than the sum of the special propositions from which it is inferred and is used to predict about unobserved cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of instances depends on number and nature, not exhaustiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Legitimacy of a generalization (induction) is determined by the number and nature of the instances examined, not by having examined every known instance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One need not have examined every known species to infer a general law; what matters is whether the sample of instances provides sufficient evidence (by their number and character) to support the induction. In contrast, a claim limited to 'all known' requires exhaustive verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing mathematical generalization from induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical 'generalizations' that summarize proved propositions (e.g., properties of conic sections) are not inductions because there is no inference to unobserved cases—the conclusion is a summing up of demonstrated premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a universal property follows deductively from the demonstrative grounds applicable to all cases (e.g., a cone can only be intersected in certain curves), the process is not inductive. Similarly, proofs via diagrams or parity of reasoning are not genuine induction because the general truth rests on demonstrative grounds rather than inference from particular observed instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a priori considerations to justify extrapolation
rubrics_metrics.description: Extending observed patterns (e.g., terms of a series) without repeating calculations is acceptable only when supported by a priori considerations that demonstrate the mode of formation will continue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mathematician may fill further terms of a series by induction only when it is apparent from a priori grounds (which could be exhibited as demonstration) that subsequent terms must follow the same rule; absent such grounds, naive extrapolation has led to false results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colligation (description) is distinct from induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Colligation (or describing a set of observed phenomena under a unifying conception) is often mistaken for induction, but it is merely summarizing or describing observed facts, not inferring unobserved facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a navigator who circumambulates and thereby describes land as an island has observed the fact (description), not induced something unknown. Kepler's representing planetary positions by an ellipse was a colligation (a mode of representing observed facts); the inductive act would be to infer unobserved intermediate positions or future positions from the observed pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: A conception must correspond to facts, not add new facts
rubrics_metrics.description: When a scientist 'introduces' a conception (e.g., ellipse) to represent observations, the conception should correspond to something actually present in the facts, rather than being an addition to the facts by the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kepler 'saw' the ellipse in the observations; he did not put it into the facts. Conceptions are often abstracted from facts; thus forming a hypothesis or model should aim to represent real properties of the phenomena, not invent them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis formation is tentative and consists of skillful guessing
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting a conception to colligate facts is a tentative, trial-and-error process of guesses; successful hypotheses are 'skillful guesses' informed by knowledge and intellectual discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kepler tried many imagined paths before the ellipse; Dr. Whewell's account that successful hypotheses are guesses is accepted, but guessing alone is invention, not proof. Hypotheses must be tested against observations and may be discarded if inconsistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction's purposes: explanation and prediction (not mere description)
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction properly belongs to operations whose aim is explanation or prediction; mere description (colligation) does not constitute induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptive schemes (e.g., circular or epicyclic models) may be adequate as representations of observed facts but differ from inductive explanations (e.g., Newtonian gravitation) which assert causes or make true predictions. Predictions that are false (e.g., eclipses as omens) illustrate a failed induction/explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colligation is necessary preparation for induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Before performing induction, detached observations must, so far as practicable, be connected by general descriptions to present phenomena as wholes; induction presupposes correct observation and suitable colligation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without prior colligation a mind could not form the basis for induction except in very limited phenomena. Good descriptive organization of facts provides the substratum on which inductive inference operates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention (framing conceptions) is not the essence of induction; proof is
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing new conceptions (invention) may be needed in studying facts but is not what constitutes induction; induction requires proof—inferring something unobserved from observed and providing tests of that inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dr. Whewell's view that invention = induction is rejected here: many inductions need no new conception beyond what is in observed instances (e.g., 'all men are mortal'). Inductive logic's special purpose is to provide tests of proof for such inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction must infer unobserved facts from observed ones
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuine inductive conclusion asserts something not directly observed — i.e., it infers unobserved facts (future occurrences, intermediate points, other members of a class) from observed instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kepler's colligation (ellipse) summarized observed positions; the real induction would be to infer that Mars occupied the unseen intermediate points or would continue to follow that path in future. If the general proposition adds nothing beyond observations, it is descriptive, not inductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction presupposes the uniformity/parallelism of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: All induction implies an assumption that there are parallel cases in nature — that what happens once will, under sufficiently similar material circumstances, happen again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the warrant underlying inference from experience. Recognizing that the universe is governed by general laws or regularities is necessary to justify generalization from particular instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify material (relevant) vs immaterial circumstances before generalizing
rubrics_metrics.description: To generalize legitimately, one must distinguish material circumstances (those relevant to the phenomenon) from immaterial ones; induction infers across cases that resemble each other in material circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill notes that how to distinguish material from immaterial circumstances is a central problem; proper induction requires specifying the description/class of cases (i.e., what aspects must be similar) for the inference to hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory inductions are singular and competing explanations are not all true
rubrics_metrics.description: While different descriptive formulations may all be 'true' representations of observed facts to varying degrees, conflicting explanations are not all true — induction as explanation must select the correct causal account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill contrasts several historical explanations of planetary motion (material wheels, vortices, Newtonian gravitation): as explanations they cannot all be true; only the correct inductive explanation (if any) withstands testing and prediction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction requires tests/proofs (canons) to distinguish true inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductive reasoning needs appropriate tests or canons of proof to establish legitimate inferences from observed cases to unobserved; mere guessing without such tests fails as induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill insists that inductive logic's role is to provide tests of proof for inferences from particulars to generals. Without such tests, the tentative invention of hypotheses does not amount to verified induction.
